result.journal: Journal of Digital Learning and Educational Innovation
result.keywords: Aim/Purpose: This study aims to examine the factors that shape student success in hybrid learning environments by integrating learner-related, technology-related, and instructional design perspectives. Background: As institutions expand blended and e-learning offerings, understanding how digital pedagogy and system quality affect learning outcomes has become increasingly important. Methodology: A survey-based design was used with undergraduate students enrolled in an introductory information systems course at a large public university in the United States. A total of 642 students responded. Contribution: The paper proposes and tests a conceptual model that combines motivation, self-regulation, platform usability, service quality, media richness, and course design to explain success in hybrid learning. Findings: Motivation and learning climate were found to be significant drivers of perceived task-technology fit and flexibility, while computer self-efficacy showed limited direct influence. Technology and system factors had consistent positive effects across outcome measures, and research-based instructional design significantly improved student capabilities. Recommendations: Educators should align digital tools with course structure and learner support mechanisms to strengthen engagement and achievement. Future Research: Subsequent studies should validate the model in different disciplines and compare fully online, blended, and face-to-face implementations.
result.title: Modeling Student Success in Hybrid Learning Environments through Research-Based Digital Pedagogy
